title: Z-RAM revival: SiGe hole well keeps floating-body charge
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died because holes stored in the floating body recombined at the source/drain junctions, and GIDL ate the sense margin as bodies shrank. Grow a 5 nm strained Si0.7Ge0.3 quantum well inside the fully depleted body under a Si cap. Holes then sit in a valence-band pocket ~0.25 eV deep, away from the high-field junction corners where they used to recombine.
why: Capacitorless 1T cell (no capacitor charge wall, 4F2-capable). Band-offset confinement is claimed to raise floating-body retention 10-100x, so refresh energy falls in proportion and the capacitor module is deleted.

title: T-RAM fixed: electrostatically doped thyristor erases dopant variability
idea: T-RAM Semiconductor's thin-capacitively-coupled thyristor died on the spread of its latch and holding voltages, caused by random implanted p-n-p-n doping. Build the thyristor in an undoped silicon nanosheet and induce its four regions with split gates (electrostatic doping). The controller trims the latch threshold per bank after test by setting gate voltages. Run the cell in dynamic mode, so data is stored as base charge rather than as holding current.
why: Removes both killers of thyristor RAM, variability and standby current. The result is a ~1-2 ns gain-read cell with no capacitor (attacks the capacitor wall), and base-charge refresh is claimed to be needed ~100x less often than DRAM refresh.

title: Optane's selector drift turned into DRAM retention
idea: In 3D XPoint, the ovonic threshold switch's threshold voltage drifted upward with log-time after each firing, which eroded read margins. Use two back-to-back OTS films as the access device of a crosspoint 1S1C capacitor cell. After each access the threshold drifts up, so the selector's off-state leakage falls as the stored bit ages. Each access or refresh re-fires the selector, which resets its state.
why: Transistor-free, stackable 4F2 crosspoint DRAM (attacks the 3D DRAM blocker and litho cost). Because drift makes leakage fall over time instead of sitting at a fixed tail, refresh is claimed to be ~10x longer than in half-select-limited crosspoint designs.

title: HPE memristor sneak paths cured by self-closing diffusive access
idea: HPE's TiO2 memristor crossbars died on sneak currents because they had no selector. Turn that failure around with an Ag-doped SiO2 diffusive memristor: it grows a filament only while a wordline pulse is applied, and the filament dissolves by itself within ~0.1-1 us. Used as a two-terminal volatile access switch in series with a stacked MIM capacitor, it gives >1e10 on/off with sub-fA off-current.
why: A two-terminal 4F2 access device that can be stacked in BEOL tiers, enabling 3D DRAM with no lateral transistor. Off-leakage far below the 13 fA tail cuts refresh 10-100x.

title: PLEDM resurrected with one epitaxial CaF2 tunnel barrier
idea: Hitachi's PLEDM vertical gain cell used a stack of Si3N4/poly-Si tunnel barriers, which made writes slow and the process complex. Replace the stack with one ~1.5 nm CaF2 barrier, grown epitaxially and lattice-matched on Si under the storage node. A surrounding gate bends the Si bands to open tunneling for writes. Because the barrier is a trap-free crystal, the off-state has no trap-assisted tunneling tail.
why: A vertical 4F2 gain cell with no capacitor, whose leakage tail is set by a crystalline barrier with no SRH or trap tail. Claimed retention is seconds, refresh is ~100x rarer, and the cell can be stacked.

title: SESO memory reborn on 2 nm single-crystal silicon nanosheets
idea: Hitachi's SESO used ~3 nm polysilicon channels: quantum confinement widened the bandgap and cut leakage to ~1e-19 A, but grain boundaries made devices variable and slow. Thin single-crystal SOI nanosheets to 2 nm with self-limiting low-temperature plasma oxidation, which raises the effective gap to ~1.6-1.8 eV. Raised epitaxial source/drain recovers the on-current.
why: Access-transistor off-current of ~1e-19 A, 5-6 decades below the 13 fA tail, made with silicon tooling. Refresh becomes ~1000x rarer and its share of idle power drops to near zero.

title: TFET's weak drive is fine for DRAM access duty
idea: Tunnel FETs failed for logic because their band-to-band on-current was too low. A DRAM access device needs only ~1 uA to charge 5 fF in 5 ns. A line-tunneling TFET (gate-overlapped pocket) has no thermionic Boltzmann tail in the off state and only weak temperature dependence. A counter-doped drain pocket suppresses ambipolar leakage.
why: The leakage tail no longer doubles every ~10 C, so the 85 C double-refresh penalty disappears. Claimed 10x longer retention in hot servers, removing most of the 16-33% of idle power spent on refresh.

title: Contactless NEMS relay: tunneling-gap mechanical access switch
idea: Nanomechanical relays died from contact wear and stiction after 1e9-1e12 cycles. Never let the beam touch: an electrostatically pulled beam moves its tip from a 4 nm gap to a 1 nm gap against the storage-node pad, which switches electron tunneling current by ~1e9 without contact. A self-assembled-monolayer stopper serves only as a fail-safe.
why: No semiconductor in the off path, so retention is limited only by the capacitor dielectric and refresh is effectively eliminated. Because the switch never makes contact, the wear that killed relays never occurs.

title: FeFET depolarization failure becomes hours-long dynamic retention
idea: FeFETs, from Bell Labs to modern devices, failed as nonvolatile memory because the depolarization field and charge trapping erased their state within days. Store the bit instead in an antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitor whose field-induced polar state is weakly stabilized by electrodes with mismatched work functions (built-in imprint). The state decays over hours rather than milliseconds, and it is read nondestructively through its field-dependent capacitance.
why: A 'slow-leak DRAM' that refreshes every few hours instead of every 32-64 ms, ~1e5x fewer refreshes. The cell never fully switches polarization, so it avoids fatigue.

title: Williams tube read-around fix: analog row-hammer integrators
idea: Williams tubes failed partly because reading one spot disturbed its neighbors (the 'read-around ratio'), so refresh had to be set by worst-case counts. Give each DRAM row driver a tiny leaky capacitor that receives a charge packet on every neighboring activation and decays over time. When its voltage crosses a comparator threshold, the driver requests a targeted refresh of that row.
why: Row-hammer protection (rows flip after ~1k ACTs) for 1T+1C+comparator per row instead of SRAM counter tables, and refresh goes only where disturbance has built up. Claimed <0.5% die area versus 2-5% for counter-based schemes.

title: Delay-line regeneration reborn as a self-timed refresh wave
idea: Mercury delay-line memories died on serial latency, but they refreshed themselves by recirculating every bit through a regenerator. Make refresh a travelling wave in the same way: each subarray refreshes one row locally, then hands a token to its neighbor, so refresh ripples continuously across the die. There are no global REF commands or all-bank stalls; the controller only sees a known 1-of-N subarray busy.
why: Recovers most of the 10-20% of bandwidth lost to refresh at 32-64 Gb and flattens peak refresh current. Scheduling moves on-die with negligible periphery.

title: CCD memory's junctionless charge wells as refresh-light storage
idea: CCD memories (Fairchild, Intel 2416) lost to DRAM on random access, but their charge sat in potential wells under gates, with no source/drain junction. Store each bit in a buried-channel well under a gate and clock it through a short 4-8 cell chain to a shared sense node. The storage node then has no p-n junction and no GIDL edge, and its only leakage is thermal generation in a fully depleted buried channel.
why: Removes junction and GIDL leakage, the dominant retention tail, for a claimed 10-100x retention gain. It also deletes 7 of every 8 access transistors (density), at the cost of a few ns of shift latency.

title: Purdue SiC DRAM revived by the EV silicon-carbide wafer glut
idea: Purdue's 1990s 4H-SiC DRAM cells held charge for years at room temperature, because the 3.26 eV gap suppresses thermal generation, but the work stalled on expensive, defect-ridden SiC wafers. EV power electronics have since made 200 mm SiC cheap. Build a planar 1T1C SiC cell with a nitrided gate oxide on U.S.-grown SiC, using spare power-device line capacity, as a refresh-free DRAM-class tier.
why: Near-nonvolatile DRAM that needs essentially no refresh, made on existing U.S. SiC capacity. Density is lower than silicon DRAM, so the gains are energy per bit and supply security, not cost per bit.

title: IBM's cryogenic dream made cheap with LNG terminal cold
idea: IBM's cryogenic Josephson computer died on refrigeration cost. At 77 K, DRAM access-transistor leakage drops by ~1e5-1e6 and refresh effectively vanishes. Site memory-heavy racks at LNG regasification terminals, which normally dump ~0.8 MJ of cold per kg into seawater, and use a nitrogen loop to hold DRAM pools at 77-100 K.
why: Eliminates refresh power and the refresh bandwidth tax, and lets access transistors use a lower Vt for speed. Cooling comes from waste cold, and leakier dies scrapped today become usable supply.

title: Vacuum tube returns as nanogap field-emission access transistor
idea: Vacuum tubes and Candescent's field-emission displays died on size, heaters and emitter non-uniformity. Use a ~20 nm vacuum-channel transistor in which a sharp source emits by Fowler-Nordheim tunneling only when the gate lowers the barrier. With no semiconductor in the channel, the off state has no thermal generation and no junction leakage, and a gap shorter than the mean free path does not need hard vacuum.
why: Off-state leakage is set by exponential FN tunneling, so it is effectively zero, and the switch is immune to temperature and radiation. Retention is limited by the capacitor dielectric, so refresh is close to eliminated.

title: TI TSRAM fixed with atomically exact 2D resonant tunneling diodes
idea: TI's tunneling SRAM added two resonant tunneling diodes to a DRAM storage node to make it static. It died on peak-current spread from monolayer thickness fluctuations in III-V barriers, and on standby current. Use graphene/hBN/graphene RTDs, whose barrier is exactly 2 or 3 atomic layers by construction, with valley current engineered to the pA level.
why: Every 1T1C node becomes a bistable latch, so refresh is eliminated at ~nW/Mb standby while 1T1C density is kept. Attacks refresh energy and the refresh bandwidth tax.

title: SONOS charge traps repurposed to trim leaky-tail access transistors
idea: SONOS and nanocrystal flash lost on retention and slow programming, neither of which matters if a cell is programmed about once a year. Add a nitride charge-trap layer to the gate stack of the buried-wordline access transistor. After retention test, use hot-carrier pulses to inject electrons into only the ~0.01% of tail transistors, raising their Vt by ~150 mV and pulling them out of the leakage tail.
why: The worst cell sets the refresh interval, so clipping the tail by 1-2 decades allows 4-8x longer refresh at 32-64 Gb. That removes most of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh cost.

title: ZettaCore molecules as built-in tunnel barrier and capacitor
idea: ZettaCore's porphyrin charge-storage molecules died on electrolyte integration and temperature limits. Covalently anchor ferrocene or porphyrin redox molecules to a TiN nanopillar through a rigid alkyl tether of chosen length, inside a solid polymer electrolyte. The tether's tunneling distance sets the self-discharge time, each CH2 unit multiplying it ~3x, so the molecular layer is both a multi-electron capacitor and its own leak-limiting access barrier.
why: Redox monolayers hold ~1e14 e/cm2, beating the MIM capacitor charge wall, and retention can be tuned from seconds to minutes by tether length. Speculative mainly because of write speed.

title: Bubble memory's rotating field drives skyrmion loops, no transistors
idea: Magnetic bubble memory died because long serial loops made access slow. Keep its best trick, one global rotating field that moves every bit so no bit needs its own transistor, and fix the latency. Use 64-bit skyrmion loops in thin multilayer rings, each with one sense MTJ, clocked by an on-chip stripline field so that any bit arrives within 64 steps.
why: The array has no access-transistor leakage and needs no refresh because it is nonvolatile, and density comes from cell-free tracks. Step speed and drive energy are the speculative parts.

title: HMC logic die justified by per-subarray negative-wordline tuning
idea: Micron's Hybrid Memory Cube died because bandwidth alone did not pay back the cost of its logic base die. Make the logic die earn its keep through leakage control. It holds per-subarray DACs and canary cells, measures the retention tail continuously, and sets each subarray's negative wordline voltage and refresh rate through hybrid-bond vias.
why: Leakage tails are local, so per-subarray NWL and refresh tuning is claimed to cut refresh energy and GIDL 2-4x versus one chip-wide setting. It also moves control logic off the DRAM die, where periphery takes 49% of the area.

title: Goto's parametron stores bits as phase in NEMS resonators
idea: The parametron, which stored bits as the oscillation phase of parametrically pumped resonators, lost to transistors on speed. Store each bit as the 0 or pi phase of a high-Q nanomechanical resonator pumped at 2f from a shared line, and read it by phase-sensitive detection. There is no leakage to fight, only pump power of roughly stored energy times omega/Q.
why: Refresh is replaced by continuous pump power, estimated at ~0.5 pW/bit for Q~1e4. That is comparable to today's refresh power but has no access-transistor tail, so retention rests on different physics. Density is speculative.

title: LPDDR partial-array self-refresh made real by OS compaction
idea: LPDDR has offered Partial Array Self-Refresh for years, but it went unused because OS allocators scatter live pages across every bank. Add a kernel 'refresh-aware compaction' pass that migrates live pages into the fewest banks before idle and marks the empty banks to the controller, which then stops refreshing them.
why: Claimed 50-80% cut in idle refresh power on phones, laptops and servers with partly free memory, with no hardware change.

title: Retired hyperscale DIMMs re-certified with a per-module retention passport
idea: Second-hand DRAM has not won trust because buyers cannot see a module's wear or retention. A test cell measures each retired DIMM's retention tail at temperature and writes a module-specific refresh multiplier and a weak-row list into its SPD. Modules with leakier access transistors then run at 2x refresh instead of being scrapped.
why: Raises usable memory supply through recycling during a ~4x price spike, handling the leakage tail with per-module refresh instead of discard.

title: HP SAIL single-stamp imprint patterns roll-to-roll oxide access arrays
idea: HP's self-aligned imprint lithography (spun out as Phicot) died chasing large display backplanes, where web stretch ruined overlay. Pattern every layer of an oxide-TFT access array on a web with one multi-height imprint stamp, etched back level by level, so the layers stay self-aligned whatever the foil distortion. Target small memory tiles that can absorb defects through redundancy.
why: Mask-free, EUV-free access devices with oxide-class leakage (<=1e-18 A) at roll-to-roll cost, for a refresh-light memory-foil tier. Capital intensity drops by orders of magnitude.

title: Organic TFT bias-stress killer neutralized by DRAM's tiny duty cycle
idea: Plastic Logic and Polymer Vision died partly because organic TFT thresholds drifted under continuous bias stress. A memory access transistor is on for only nanoseconds per refresh period (duty ~1e-7), and the retention bias can be chosen to anneal any drift back out. Print a wide-gap (~3 eV) small-molecule semiconductor whose tiny intrinsic carrier density gives sub-fA off-current.
why: A printable, solution-coated access device with very low leakage, giving refresh intervals of seconds on foil. It is built from abundant carbon chemistry instead of tungsten-heavy, EUV-patterned stacks.

title: Intel-Opticom polymer ferroelectric becomes a zero-refresh sleep shadow
idea: Intel and Opticom's printed P(VDF-TrFE) polymer memory failed as main memory because of microsecond switching, fatigue and disturb. Print it instead as a per-row shadow layer over an oxide-TFT memory foil. When the foil enters sleep, each row copies itself into its polymer shadow (slow, rare writes), and power and refresh drop to zero. On wake, the rows restore.
why: Eliminates refresh energy during idle. Fatigue stops mattering at ~1e4 sleep cycles over a lifetime, and the shadow is an additive printed layer.

title: Rolltronics plastic failure fixed with roll-to-roll flexible glass anneal
idea: Rolltronics' roll-to-roll a-Si TFTs on plastic died on substrate shrinkage and the low process temperatures plastic allows. Build oxide access TFTs on rolls of ~100 um flexible glass, which tolerate 450 C anneals. Those anneals drive out the oxygen vacancies and hydrogen that set the oxide-TFT leakage tail.
why: Hot-annealed oxide channels are claimed to have a 10-100x tighter leakage tail than plastic-limited ones, which makes refresh-free printed memory foils credible.

title: Graphene's roll-to-roll CVD line repurposed for MoS2 access channels
idea: Graphene transistors failed as switches because graphene has no bandgap, yet roll-to-roll CVD growth and transfer of graphene worked. Reuse those R2R furnaces and transfer lines to grow monolayer MoS2 (1.8 eV gap) on metal foil and laminate it onto capacitor foils as the access channel.
why: An atomically thin, wide-gap access channel: off-current approaches 1e-18 A/um with good electrostatics at short channels. R2R processing cuts capital per square meter.

title: IBM nanotube logic failure recast as printed foil refresh periphery
idea: IBM's carbon-nanotube transistor program stalled because logic needed perfect tube placement and purity. Printed random networks of semiconducting CNTs make p-type TFTs that tolerate that randomness. Paired with printed n-type oxide TFTs, they form complementary circuits on the foil for per-tile sense amplifiers and refresh/ECC controllers next to the oxide access arrays.
why: Putting refresh periphery on the foil removes silicon companion chips, and CMOS on foil keeps standby power low. Manufacturable roll-to-roll in the U.S.

title: Konarka's moisture death avoided via roll-to-roll spatial-ALD ultrabarrier
idea: Konarka's roll-to-roll organic PV died largely from water and oxygen leaking through weak barriers. Deposit a 20 nm Al2O3/ZrO2 nanolaminate by R2R spatial ALD (WVTR <1e-6 g/m2/day) directly over the oxide access TFTs. It also blocks in-diffusing hydrogen, which acts as a donor and raises off-current.
why: Stops the leakage tail from drifting in the field, the main reliability risk of printed oxide memory, so a long refresh interval set at test stays valid for years.

title: Nanosolar's aluminum foil anodized into capacitor pores with diode floors
idea: Nanosolar's roll-to-roll CIGS on aluminium foil died on efficiency, but its cheap Al-foil web still works. Anodize the foil roll into self-ordered alumina pores at 100 nm pitch and 60:1 aspect ratio, and line them by ALD as MIM capacitors. Stepping down the anodization voltage at the end thins each pore floor's barrier layer to ~2 nm (about 1.2 nm per volt), forming a self-aligned MIIM tunnel diode as each cell's access element.
why: Attacks the capacitor wall with high-aspect-ratio pores that need no etch tool, plus an electrochemically defined access barrier. Aluminium is abundant (no tungsten) and the process is roll-to-roll.

title: Nanotube-source vertical transistor leakage fixed with capped-source access
idea: Carbon-nanotube-source vertical organic transistors (the CN-VFET line of startups) died on high off-current that flowed straight through the porous source. Electrodeposit a 5 nm insulating cap selectively on top of the printed nanotube mesh, so carriers inject only at the mesh edges under gate control. The result is a vertical, printable access device whose channel length is a film thickness (~100 nm).
why: A short-channel, printable vertical access device with ~1e9 on/off, fast enough for ~100 ns foil memory. It fits compact near-4F2 footprints without lithography.

title: Single-electron memory variability averaged out by printed Au55 cluster arrays
idea: Single-electron memories died because random background charges shifted each Coulomb-blockade island's threshold. Print a dense monolayer of ligand-capped ~1.4 nm gold clusters between storage node and bitline. Thousands of junctions in series and parallel average out the offset charges, and the room-temperature blockade (~0.2-0.3 eV charging energy) blocks conduction below threshold.
why: A printable two-terminal access element with exponential sub-threshold suppression and no semiconductor generation current, a new leakage physics. Speculative.

title: Kodak spatial-ALD with inkjet inhibitors prints maskless low-leakage channels
idea: Kodak's selective-area spatial ALD for printed electronics was shelved along with its display ambitions. Inkjet a polymer inhibitor pattern onto a moving web, then grow ZnO/IGZO and Al2O3 by ALD only where the inhibitor is absent. Access TFTs are built additively with ALD-grade interfaces instead of solution-processed oxide.
why: ALD interfaces give leakage close to vacuum-deposited oxide (<=1e-18 A) while staying printable and maskless, with no photoresist or litho capex. Builds on existing Rochester-area U.S. know-how.

title: RCA Selectron flood-gun holding rebuilt as optically held printed cells
idea: RCA's Selectron used a continuous flood electron beam to hold every bit (secondary emission made two potentials stable), but the tubes could not be manufactured. Print each cell as a storage node with two organic photoconductors that the node's own voltage gates, giving positive feedback. A uniform low-power LED flood then continuously restores both 1s and 0s, with no row cycling and no sense amps.
why: Refresh is replaced by photonic holding: no refresh commands, no bandwidth tax, no refresh periphery. The photoconductor stacks are printed.

title: Nextreme thin-film thermoelectrics revived to dodge 85C refresh doubling
idea: Nextreme's thin-film thermoelectric coolers faded because of poor efficiency. Refresh doubles above 85 C, so even a low-COP cooler pays off if it shaves the last 5-10 C. Screen-print Bi2Te3-based thermoelectric films onto DIMM and HBM heat spreaders and turn them on only when the die sensors approach 80 C.
why: Keeps hot accelerator memory in 1x refresh, avoiding the extra ~46 fJ/bit of refresh and ~10% of bandwidth that 2x refresh costs. Printable and cheap.

title: Dead body-bias trick revived via printed back-gate planes
idea: Dynamic body biasing (DTMOS) died in bulk CMOS because the body-effect coefficient shrank and wells are huge capacitors. In a printed double-gate oxide TFT array, a printed global back-gate plane couples strongly to the thin channel. Hold the plane at -3 V during retention (high Vt, ultralow leakage) and swing it to 0 V only on the tile being accessed (low Vt, fast).
why: Decouples speed from leakage, so access devices can be fast and still retain for seconds. Cuts refresh ~100x on foil memory.

title: Semprius transfer printing puts crystalline access transistors on printed capacitors
idea: Semprius's micro-transfer printing died with concentrated PV, not because the stamps failed. Release arrays of single-crystal SOI access transistors (long channel, thick oxide, low leakage) from a donor wafer and stamp them onto a capacitor foil made roll-to-roll. The donor's handle wafer is reused for many foils.
why: Crystalline, low-leakage switches without building a DRAM fab, with capacitors made roll-to-roll. Handle reuse lowers demand for Cz silicon and crucibles.

title: Solexel's porous-silicon lift-off foils as crucible-free low-leakage substrates
idea: Solexel's kerfless epitaxial silicon foils died against cheap Chinese wafers. Grow 20-40 um of epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer, lift it off, and handle the foils roll-to-roll on carrier tape, reusing each template ~50x. Epi silicon carries little oxygen and metal, so access-transistor junction leakage is lower than on Cz.
why: Fewer Cz ingots mean less demand for Spruce Pine high-purity quartz crucibles, and epi material tightens the retention tail. Gives a U.S.-manufacturable foil supply.

title: Core memory's hand-threading killed it; print planar ferrite cores
idea: Ferrite core memory died because the cores had to be threaded by hand. Print soft-ferrite nanoparticle rings in planar form on a web, with screen-printed silver X, Y and sense windings, and read them by coincident-current half-select. There is no access transistor, so there is no leakage and no refresh.
why: A transistor-free, refresh-free, radiation-hard working-memory tier made roll-to-roll from abundant iron oxide. Density is low (~1 Mb/cm2), so the targets are edge and defense uses and supply diversity.

title: Orphaned flexible-display pilot lines become a national printed memory foundry
idea: U.S. flexible display programs, such as the Army-funded Flexible Display Center, never found an anchor product. Re-task such roll-to-roll oxide-TFT lines into a federally backed pilot foundry for refresh-free oxide memory foils, with DoD as anchor buyer for low-power ruggedized memory.
why: Supplies the anchor customer whose absence killed U.S. flexible electronics, and creates U.S.-made DRAM-adjacent capacity without $15B fabs or EUV.

title: Printed-electronics bust fixed by toll-printing memory foil on converters
idea: The 2008-2012 printed-electronics boom went bust because startups built their own lines to make low-value labels. Instead, license a memory-foil recipe (printed oxide access devices plus capacitors) to U.S. flexible-packaging converters whose roll-to-roll lines run below capacity, and pay them per m2 of good foil.
why: Near-zero capital per unit of capacity because it uses idle presses, so supply can scale fast. Low-leakage printed access devices make the foil refresh-light, so it ships with only a simple controller.

title: Kovio printed silicon diode pairs as two-way crosspoint access
idea: Kovio's printed-silicon RFID died because printed tags had to undercut cheap silicon chips. Use its cyclopentasilane ink, crystallized by flash lamp, to print two opposing p-i-n diodes per cell, one to a write-1 line and one to a write-0 line. When idle, the storage node is isolated by two reverse-biased diodes, giving a transistor-free crosspoint 2D1C cell.
why: Printable access with no transistor, with leakage set by reverse diode current, and the cells can be stacked in printed tiers. Memory's value per m2 justifies the cost of printed silicon where RFID's did not.

title: NVDIMM-N failure fixed with printed zinc battery self-refresh
idea: NVDIMM-N modules died on the cost of their flash, supercapacitors and backup controller. Laminate a printed zinc-manganese battery film onto the DIMM that keeps the DRAM in self-refresh through a power loss for minutes to an hour, with no copy to flash.
why: Makes DRAM survive outages for pennies per module, so servers can drop a separate persistence tier. Refresh is carried by stored energy instead of a flash backup.

title: Thinfilm's yield problem solved by self-clearing printed electrodes
idea: Thinfilm's printed memories struggled with yield because of pinholes and leaky spots. Borrow the self-healing of metallized-film capacitors: print 20 nm aluminium top electrodes, so that during a burn-in pulse any leakage hot spot heats up and vaporizes the electrode around it. That disconnects the leaky cell, which is then mapped out instead of setting the retention time.
why: Physically clips the leakage tail of printed arrays, so refresh is set by intrinsic leakage rather than defects. Printable.

title: Resistive-load 4T SRAM revived with printed oxide TFT loads
idea: The 4T SRAM with polysilicon load resistors died because its TOhm loads would not scale and drew standby current. Oxide semiconductors lack a good p-type, so they cannot make CMOS SRAM, but they make superb loads. Print a cross-coupled pair of oxide TFTs whose loads are oxide TFTs in deep subthreshold, sized so the load current (~1e-15 A) exceeds pull-down leakage (~1e-18 A).
why: A static, refresh-free, n-type-only printed cell with ~fW standby per bit, which gets around oxide electronics' missing p-type.
